subject: Cash or financed? Model the same deal both ways
preheader: A timeless comparison framework for liquidity, debt service, and property-level risk

marketSnapshot.headline: Cash and financing change the capital stack—not the property
marketSnapshot.body: There is no universal winner. A cash purchase removes scheduled debt service but commits more capital to one asset. Financing preserves liquidity but adds payment, rate, maturity, and lender constraints. Compare both versions with the same property inputs, then replace every financing placeholder with a current quote before making a decision.

dealSpotter.body: Model the purchase price, closing cash, reserves, rent, vacancy, operating expenses, and future capital needs. Removing debt service can improve modeled monthly cash flow, but it does not remove operating, tenant, insurance, title, liquidity, or concentration risk.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Lower initial equity, added debt obligations
dealSpotter.body: Use the same property assumptions, then enter the proposed down payment, rate, term, mortgage insurance, fees, and any maturity or balloon terms from the actual financing proposal. Compare cash required, recurring cash flow, DSCR, and cash-on-cash return without treating the model as lender approval.

A modeled return does not answer how much liquidity you should retain. Stress-test vacancy, repairs, insurance, taxes, and rate changes, then review the resulting cash needs against your broader finances and risk tolerance with qualified professionals where appropriate.

blogFeature.title: Cash-on-cash vs IRR — what each metric measures
blogFeature.excerpt: Cash-on-cash focuses on modeled annual cash flow relative to initial cash invested. IRR is a longer-horizon modeled return that depends on timing and exit assumptions. Neither metric is a recommendation.

qa.question: How should I compare an all-cash purchase with a financed purchase?
qa.answer: Run the same property twice and change only the financing inputs. Compare total cash required, recurring cash flow, DSCR when debt exists, cash-on-cash return, liquidity remaining after closing, and downside scenarios. Replace the national rate benchmark with current investment-property quotes and include lender fees and loan terms. The appropriate capital structure depends on the property, available financing, reserves, taxes, portfolio concentration, and your risk tolerance; confirm financing, tax, and legal consequences with the relevant professionals.
